SECTION 3: SITUATIONAL SALES SCENARIOS
SITUATION 1: First-Time Client Inquiry (Phone)
Scenario: Potential client calls asking about Botox pricing
Who Handles: Front Desk
Objectives:
●      Avoid pricing in isolation
●      Position value before cost
●      Secure consultation
●      Plant package/membership seed
Complete Script Flow:
Client: "Hi, how much is Botox?"
Front Desk: "Great question! I'm so glad you called. My name is [Name]. Who do I have the pleasure of speaking with?"
Client: "[Name]"
Front Desk: "Wonderful, [Name]. I love that you're thinking about this. Before I talk numbers, can I ask — is this your first time considering neurotoxin treatments, or have you had Botox before?"
Client Response A: "First time"
Front Desk: "Perfect! So here's what I recommend: Botox is typically priced per unit, and everyone needs a different amount based on their goals and muscle strength. Rather than throw a random number at you, let's get you in for a complimentary consultation with one of our injectors. They'll assess exactly what you need, show you what's possible, and give you precise pricing. Most clients find this way more helpful than a phone quote. Do mornings or afternoons work better for you?"
Client Response B: "I've had it before"
Front Desk: "Awesome! So you know how it works. Our pricing is $12 per unit, and most clients use between 20-60 units depending on the areas they treat. That said, we also offer packages and a membership that brings your cost down significantly — especially if you're maintaining this regularly. Would you like to come in and speak with an injector about a long-term plan, or would you prefer to just book a single treatment?"
Key Teaching Points:
●      Never give pricing without context
●      Always offer consultation for new clients
●      For returning clients, mention packages immediately
●      Use assumptive language ("when" not "if")

SITUATION 2: Client Books Single Treatment Online
Scenario: Client self-schedules a single laser hair removal session via website
Who Handles: Front Desk (confirmation call) → Consultant (day-of)
Objectives:
●      Educate on treatment series requirements
●      Position package before arrival
●      Set expectation for consultation upsell
Front Desk Confirmation Call Script:
Front Desk: "Hi [Name], this is [Your Name] from [Practice]. I'm calling to confirm your laser hair removal appointment on [Date] at [Time]. Do you have a quick second?"
Client: "Yes"
Front Desk: "Perfect! I just want to make sure you have the right expectations. Laser hair removal isn't a one-and-done treatment — it typically takes 6-8 sessions for permanent reduction. Most of our clients purchase a package upfront because it saves money and ensures they complete the full series. When you come in, your consultant will go over the options with you. Sound good?"
Client: "Okay, yes"
Front Desk: "Great! We'll see you [Day] at [Time]. Looking forward to meeting you!"
Day-of Consultant Script:
Consultant: "Hi [Name]! Welcome. I see you're here for laser hair removal. Have you done this before, or is this your first time?"
Client: "First time"
Consultant: "Perfect. So here's what you need to know: one session will reduce some hair, but you won't see permanent results. Hair grows in cycles, so we need to catch it multiple times. The gold standard is 6-8 treatments, spaced 4-6 weeks apart. We have a few options:
●      Single session: $350
●      Package of 6: $1,800 (saves $300)
●      Package of 8: $2,400 (saves $400 and ensures complete results)
Most clients go with the 6 or 8 because they want this done right. Which makes more sense for your goals?"
Key Teaching Points:
●      Educate before they arrive
●      Frame packages as the standard, not an upsell
●      Use savings language
●      Give clear options with recommendation

SITUATION 3: Client Hesitant About Package Pricing
Scenario: Client wants results but resists package investment
Who Handles: Consultant, Esthetician, Nurse, or Injector (whoever is presenting)
Objectives:
●      Reframe from cost to value
●      Break down cost-per-result
●      Offer payment plans
●      Compare to doing nothing
Complete Objection Handling Script:
Client: "That's more than I wanted to spend"
You: "I totally understand — I want to make sure you're comfortable. Can I ask, what were you thinking investment-wise?"
Client: "I was hoping to just do one and see"
You: "That makes sense, and you absolutely can. Here's what I want you to know: when clients do one treatment, they see some improvement, but it's temporary. Then they come back six months later and we're starting over. The clients who get the results they actually want are the ones who commit to the full series upfront. So it's less about spending more — it's about actually solving the problem versus just renting a solution. Does that make sense?"
Client: "Yeah, but I still don't know if I can afford it right now"
You: "Totally fair. We do offer payment plans — you can spread this over [X] months, which brings it down to about [Y] per month. That's less than most people spend on coffee. And honestly, if this is important to you, isn't it worth financing a real solution rather than wasting money on things that don't work?"
Alternative Approach (Budget-Conscious):
You: "I hear you. Let me ask — what's your timeline? Are you trying to see results for a specific event, or is this more of a general goal?"
Client: "I just want to look better"
You: "Got it. So here's another option: we have a membership that spreads the cost out monthly and gets you access to multiple services at a lower rate. A lot of clients find that easier to budget for. Want me to walk you through it?"
Key Teaching Points:
●      Never argue, always empathize first
●      Reframe cost as investment in results
●      Offer payment plans immediately
●      Compare to cost of NOT solving the problem

SITUATION 4: Retail Recommendation During Facial
Scenario: Esthetician performing facial on client with visible hyperpigmentation
Who Handles: Esthetician
Objectives:
●      Tie retail to treatment outcomes
●      Position as essential, not optional
●      Recommend full routine, not single product
●      Overcome "I'll think about it"
Treatment Room Script:
During Treatment:
Esthetician: "So while we're working on your skin today, I'm noticing some hyperpigmentation around your cheeks and forehead. Is that something you've been trying to address?"
Client: "Yeah, I've tried a few things but nothing really works"
Esthetician: "That makes sense — hyperpigmentation is stubborn. The good news is, what we're doing in-clinic today will help, but if we don't support it at home, the results won't last. I'm going to recommend a few products that actually work. Sound good?"
Client: "Sure"
At End of Treatment:
Esthetician: "Okay, so here's what your skin needs. I'm recommending three things:
Vitamin C serum in the morning — this brightens and prevents new spots
Retinol at night — this accelerates cell turnover and fades existing spots
SPF 50 daily — because UV exposure will undo everything
These three together are what all my clients with hyperpigmentation use, and they see results in about 4-6 weeks. The investment is about $180 total, and these will last you 3-4 months. Do you want to start with the full routine or just pick one?"
Client: "That's expensive. Can I just get the Vitamin C?"
Esthetician: "You can, but here's the thing — if you only do one, you won't see the results you want. It's like going to the gym once a week and expecting a six-pack. These products work together. If budget is the concern, I'd rather you start with the retinol and SPF, because those will give you more visible improvement. But ideally, all three."
Client: "Let me think about it"
Esthetician: "Of course! But can I be honest? Every client who says 'let me think about it' either forgets, or buys something random at Target that doesn't work, and then we're back here having the same conversation in three months. You're already investing in facials — let's make sure that investment actually pays off. If you get these today, I'll follow up with you in a month and we'll see what's working. Deal?"
Key Teaching Points:
●      Diagnose the problem during treatment
●      Recommend a complete system, not a single product
●      Tie to treatment they're already paying for
●      Overcome objections with truth and urgency

Scenario: Client books Botox but would benefit from filler, skin tightening, or full-face plan

Key Teaching Points:
●      Use discovery questions to uncover full needs
●      Educate with mirror/visual tools
●      Present tiered options with clear recommendation
●      Don't back down from full plan, but offer staged approach

CATEGORY 1: Injectable Services (Botox, Dysport, Filler)

SECTION 6: OBJECTION HANDLING FRAMEWORK
OBJECTION 1: "I need to think about it"
What It Usually Means:
●      Price concern
●      Need to consult spouse/partner
●      Lack of urgency
●      Unclear value
Response Template:
"I totally understand — this is an important decision. Can I ask what specifically you want to think about? Is it the investment, the timing, or something about the treatment plan?"
If Price: "Let me ask — if money weren't an issue, would you move forward today?" [If yes] → Offer payment plan [If no] → Dig deeper into real objection
If Partner: "That makes sense. What questions do you think [partner] will have? Let me give you everything you need to have that conversation." [Provide take-home materials, pricing breakdown, before/after photos]
If Value Unclear: "Let me make sure I've explained this clearly — here's exactly what you're getting and why it works..."
Closing: "Here's what I know: clients who go home to think about it either forget, or they talk themselves out of something that would really help them. If this is important to you, let's at least get you scheduled so you don't lose your spot. You can always change your mind. Fair?"

OBJECTION 2: "That's too expensive"
What It Usually Means:
●      Didn't understand value
●      Comparing to wrong benchmark
●      Can't afford it (real or perceived)
Response Template:
"I appreciate you being honest with me. Can I ask — what were you hoping to invest?"
[Listen to answer]
"Okay, so here's the thing: [treatment] isn't cheap, but it's also not expensive when you compare it to [alternative]. Let me break it down..."

"This package is $3,000 for six months of results. That's $500/month — less than most people spend on gym memberships they don't use."
"You could do single sessions at $400 each and spend $2,400 total, or you could do the package for $1,800 and save $600. Which makes more sense?"
"If we don't fix this now, you'll spend the next five years buying products that don't work. This actually solves the problem."
Payment Plan Transition:
"If budget is the concern, we offer payment plans. You could spread this over [X] months for about $[Y] per month. Does that make it more manageable?"

OBJECTION 3: "I want to try one first"
What It Usually Means:
●      Fear of commitment
●      Testing your credibility
●      Lack of trust in results
Response Template:
"I completely understand the hesitation. Let me ask — if you do one session and love it, what happens next?"
Client: "I'll come back for more"
You: "Exactly. So here's what happens: you do one, you see some improvement, you come back, and you pay full price for the rest. Or, you commit to the series now, save money, and actually get the results you want. The series isn't just about saving money — it's about ensuring you finish what you start. Make sense?"
Alternative Approach:
"Here's what I see happen: clients try one, love it, but then life gets busy. Six months later they're back at square one. The clients who get results are the ones who commit upfront. I want you to be in the second group."

OBJECTION 4: "I'll just do it somewhere cheaper"
What It Usually Means:
●      Found Groupon/discount competitor
●      Doesn't understand quality differences
Response Template:
"I totally get it — there are definitely cheaper options out there. Can I ask where you're seeing lower prices?"
[Listen]

Quality Differentiation:
"Our [equipment] is medical-grade and FDA-approved. Our injectors have [X years experience]. Our products are pharmaceutical-grade. That costs more, but it's also why our results last longer and look better."
Closing:
"You're going to pay for this one way or another — either you pay less upfront and more later to fix it, or you invest properly now and get it right the first time. What do you want to do?"

OBJECTION 5: "I don't have time for multiple appointments"
What It Usually Means:
●      Busy schedule
●      Doesn't want commitment
●      Needs flexibility
Response Template:
"I hear you — everyone's busy. Let me ask: would you rather come in six times over six months and actually solve this, or keep living with [problem] because you're too busy to fix it?"
Reframe:
"We schedule appointments around your life. Most clients come in every [X weeks] — that's 30 minutes out of your month. You'll spend more time scrolling Instagram today than you will in this chair. Is it really a time issue, or is it something else?"
Offer Solution:
"Let's book your appointments in advance for days that work for you. If something comes up, we'll move it. But at least you're committed to the plan. Sound fair?"

Single session (least value)
Mid-tier package (good value)

SITUATION 1: First-Time Client Inquiry (Phone)

Complete Script Flow:
Client: "Hi, how much is Botox?"

Client: "[Name]"
Front Desk: "Wonderful, [Name]. I love that you're thinking about this. Before I talk numbers, can I ask — is this your first time considering neurotoxin treatments, or have you had Botox before?"
Client Response A: "First time"
Front Desk: "Perfect! So here's what I recommend: Botox is typically priced per unit, and everyone needs a different amount based on their goals and muscle strength. Rather than throw a random number at you, let's get you in for a complimentary consultation with one of our injectors. Client Response B: "I've had it before"

That said, we also offer packages and a membership that brings your cost down significantly — especially if you're maintaining this regularly. Would you like to come in and speak with an injector about a long-term plan, or would you prefer to just book a single treatment?"
Key Teaching Points:
●      Never give pricing without context
●      Always offer consultation for new clients
●      For returning clients, mention packages immediately
●      Use assumptive language ("when" not "if")

SITUATION 2: Client Books Single Treatment Online
Scenario: Client self-schedules a single laser hair removal session via website
Who Handles: Front Desk (confirmation call) → Consultant (day-of)
Objectives:
●      Educate on treatment series requirements
●      Position package before arrival
●      Set expectation for consultation upsell

Client: "Yes"
Front Desk: "Perfect! I just want to make sure you have the right expectations. Laser hair removal isn't a one-and-done treatment — it typically takes 6-8 sessions for permanent reduction. Most of our clients purchase a package upfront because it saves money and ensures they complete the full series. When you come in, your consultant will go over the options with you. Sound good?"
Client: "Okay, yes"
Front Desk: "Great! We'll see you [Day] at [Time]. Looking forward to meeting you!"
Day-of Consultant Script:
Consultant: "Hi [Name]! Welcome. I see you're here for laser hair removal. Have you done this before, or is this your first time?"
Client: "First time"
Consultant: "Perfect. So here's what you need to know: one session will reduce some hair, but you won't see permanent results. Hair grows in cycles, so we need to catch it multiple times. The gold standard is 6-8 treatments, spaced 4-6 weeks apart. We have a few options:
●      Single session: $350
●      Package of 6: $1,800 (saves $300)
●      Package of 8: $2,400 (saves $400 and ensures complete results)
Most clients go with the 6 or 8 because they want this done right. Which makes more sense for your goals?"
Key Teaching Points:
●      Educate before they arrive
●      Frame packages as the standard, not an upsell
●      Use savings language
●      Give clear options with recommendation

●      Break down cost-per-result
●      Offer payment plans
●      Compare to doing nothing

You: "I totally understand — I want to make sure you're comfortable. Can I ask, what were you thinking investment-wise?"
Client: "I was hoping to just do one and see"
You: "That makes sense, and you absolutely can. Here's what I want you to know: when clients do one treatment, they see some improvement, but it's temporary. Script: "Botox handles movement lines beautifully. But I'm noticing some volume loss here and here. If we add just one syringe of filler, you'll look 5 years younger instead of just smoother. Want to do both?"
C. Single Treatment → Package
Scenario: Client paying per visit

CATEGORY 2: Laser & Energy-Based Treatments
Who Can Upsell: Consultants, Estheticians, Nurses, Providers

SECTION 6: OBJECTION HANDLING FRAMEWORK
OBJECTION 1: "I need to think about it"
What It Usually Means:
●      Price concern
●      Need to consult spouse/partner
●      Lack of urgency
●      Unclear value
Response Template:

If Partner: "That makes sense. What questions do you think [partner] will have? Let me give you everything you need to have that conversation." [Provide take-home materials, pricing breakdown, before/after photos]
If Value Unclear: "Let me make sure I've explained this clearly — here's exactly what you're getting and why it works..."
Closing: "Here's what I know: clients who go home to think about it either forget, or they talk themselves out of something that would really help them. If this is important to you, let's at least get you scheduled so you don't lose your spot. You can always change your mind. Fair?"

OBJECTION 2: "That's too expensive"
What It Usually Means:
●      Didn't understand value
●      Comparing to wrong benchmark
●      Can't afford it (real or perceived)
Response Template:

You are an expert sales trainer for [YOUR MEDSPA NAME], a luxury medical spa specializing in [YOUR SERVICES]. You have been trained on The Luxora Collective's Lifetime Value Sales & Client Experience Playbook.

[Insert your mission statement or core values]

   - Closing techniques

- Sales is service, service is sales
- Education eliminates buyer's remorse
- Recommend the complete solution, not the minimum
- Confidence is required to build trust
- Never use pressure tactics
- Every visit should have a next step
- Packages and memberships serve client outcomes
- Lifetime value beats transactional thinking
 
TONE & STYLE:
- Professional but conversational
- Confident and directive
- Empathetic to both client and staff concerns
- Focused on win-win outcomes
- Educational rather than pushy
 
When staff interact with you, respond as if you're their sales coach sitting right next to them, ready to help them navigate any client conversation with confidence and success.

How to Use This Template
Step 1: Fill in all bracketed sections with your specific information
Step 2: Add this prompt to your practice's ChatGPT, Claude, or internal AI tool
Step 3: Train your team to use it by:
●      Asking for scripts before difficult conversations

Step 4: Update the prompt quarterly based on:
●      New services or pricing

FINAL LUXORA STANDARDS
The Non-Negotiables
Every client interaction must include:
Warm, professional greeting
Discovery questions that uncover true goals
Education tied to outcomes, not just features
Recommendation of complete solution (not minimum)
Discussion of package or membership if applicable
Next step secured (appointment, retail purchase, or follow-up)
No client should ever leave without:
Understanding their treatment plan
Knowing what happens next
Feeling educated and confident
Having an opportunity to commit to packages/membership
If a client exits with no plan, no education, and no follow-up, that is a system failure.

Quality Assurance Checklist

●      Review missed opportunities from previous day
●      Huddle on any difficult client conversations
●      Celebrate wins and package sales
Weekly:
●      Team meeting to review metrics
●      Role-play challenging scenarios
●      Share success stories
Monthly:

●      Identify training gaps
●      Update scripts based on results
●      Recognize top performers
Quarterly:
●      Comprehensive playbook review
●      Update pricing and packages
●      Refresh training
●      Set new revenue goals

CONCLUSION
This playbook is not a suggestion. It is a system.
When implemented with fidelity, it will:
●      Increase average transaction value by 40-60%
●      Improve client retention by 30-50%
●      Create predictable recurring revenue through memberships
●      Build a culture where sales feels natural, not forced
●      Transform your team into confident, ethical revenue generators
The difference between a good medspa and a great one isn't the services you offer.
It's how confidently and completely you guide clients to the right solution.
Sales is service. Service is sales.
Now go serve at the highest level.

The Luxora Collective Growth Partner to High-Integrity MedSpas

**Treatment Pairing Principles**

**Pairing Rule #1: Mechanism Complementarity**  
Combine treatments that work through different biological mechanisms for additive results.

Example: Botox (muscle relaxation) + Sculptra (collagen stimulation) + IPL (pigment reduction)  
Why it works: Each addresses different aging mechanisms without overlap or interference

**Pairing Rule #2: Timeline Synchronization**  
Bundle treatments that share optimal spacing intervals.

Example:
• Microneedling + PRP (sessions every 4 weeks)  
• Laser hair removal + skin tightening (sessions every 6 weeks)  
• Botox + dermal fillers (maintenance every 12 weeks)

**Pairing Rule #3: Pre-Treatment Enhancement**  
Include preparatory services that improve primary treatment outcomes.

Example: Hydrafacial before laser resurfacing - clears surface debris for better laser penetration

**Pairing Rule #4: Post-Treatment Optimization**  
Add supportive modalities that accelerate healing and extend results.

Example: LED therapy after chemical peels - reduces inflammation, accelerates cellular repair

**Pairing Rule #5: Cross-Category Synergy**  
Combine face + body, internal + external, or active + passive treatments.

Example: "The Total Reset"
• Injectable neurotoxins (face)  
• Body contouring (physique)  
• IV nutrient therapy (internal wellness)  
• Professional skincare (daily maintenance)

**SECTION 3: MEMBERSHIP PSYCHOLOGY**

**The 7 Behavioral Triggers That Lock in Commitment**

**1. Sunk Cost Effect**  
Psychology: Once invested, people justify continued participation  
Application: Monthly payments create ongoing psychological investment  
Design Principle: Automatic recurring billing (never one-time annual only)

**2. Loss Aversion**  
Psychology: Fear of losing benefits outweighs desire to gain new ones  
Application: "Unused credits expire" creates urgency to schedule  
Design Principle: Rolling credits with expiration (2-4 months max)

**3. Endowment Effect**  
Psychology: People value what they "own" more highly  
Application: Members feel ownership over "their" credits and benefits  
Design Principle: Personalized member portals showing "Your Credits" and "Your Savings"

**4. Social Proof & Status**  
Psychology: Desire to belong to exclusive groups  
Application: VIP/Elite tier naming, member-only events  
Design Principle: Visible status indicators (different colored member cards, priority lanes)

**5. Goal Gradient Effect**  
Psychology: Motivation increases as people approach goals  
Application: Tiered progression system encourages upgrades  
Design Principle: "You're only $X away from Platinum benefits!"

**6. Reciprocity Principle**  
Psychology: People feel obligated to give back when they receive  
Application: Birthday gifts, surprise upgrades, free samples  
Design Principle: Unexpected perks that create "wow" moments

**7. Paradox of Choice**  
Psychology: Too many options paralyze decisions  
Application: 3-4 clear tiers (not 7-8 confusing options)  
Design Principle: Simple, differentiated value propositions per tier
